description: Western ulus of the Mongol Empire (1242–1502) dominating the Pontic steppe and forcing tribute from Russian principalities; its Islamisation under Özbeg Khan (1313) reoriented it away from the eastern Mongol world, while its commercial cities, Sarai, Caffa, Tana, were nodes in the Eurasian trade network linking China to the Mediterranean.

temporal.notes: Mongol successor khanate; major influence on Russian principalities

lifecycle_phases.description: Batu Khan leads Mongol armies through Russia (1237–1238) and Eastern Europe (1241); establishes the Golden Horde on the Pontic-Caspian steppe with the capital at Sarai. Russian principalities become tributaries, ending the Kievan political system.

Dominates the Pontic steppe, controls Russian principalities, and trades extensively with Genoese colonies on the Black Sea. Khan Öz Beg (1313–1341) converts the khanate to Islam, giving it new ideological coherence. Taxes from Russian tribute and transit trade make Sarai one of the largest cities in the world.

Battle of Kulikovo (1380), Moscow defeats a Golden Horde army for the first time. Timur (Tamerlane) devastates the khanate (1395–1396). The Great Horde fragments into Kazan, Crimean, Astrakhan, and Siberian khanates; Moscow ends tribute payment in 1480.

rise_factors.description: Mongol cavalry and decimal organization overwhelmed the fragmented Russian principalities and Polish-Hungarian forces; superior strategic mobility allowed rapid conquest of territories from China to Poland
Control of the northern Silk Road routes and Genoese Black Sea colonies made Sarai a major commercial hub; tribute from Russian principalities provided steady revenue
Russian principalities were internally divided and unable to coordinate military resistance; the Kievan political system had already fragmented before the Mongol invasion

The Golden Horde controlled the Volga River from its source to the Caspian Sea, taxing the most lucrative Eurasian overland trade route. Sarai (capital near modern Astrakhan) became a major commercial city processing goods between China and the Black Sea.

The Golden Horde's census and taxation system (based on Chinese administrative models) extracted systematic tribute from Russian principalities. The revenue from dozens of Russian cities funded Mongol military campaigns across the steppe.

Batu Khan integrated the defeated Kipchak (Cuman) steppe cavalry into his armies, doubling the military manpower of the western Mongol khanate. These seasoned nomadic warriors provided the Golden Horde with sustainable military capacity beyond its original Mongol core.

decline_factors.description: The Black Death (1346–1348) devastated the steppe populations and commercial cities; repeated outbreaks throughout the 14th century reduced the taxable and military population

The Great Troubles (1359–1380) saw rapid turnover of khans and civil war; the Battle of Kulikovo (1380) showed Russian princes could resist; Timur's invasions (1395–1396) destroyed Sarai and disrupted trade routes permanently

Persistent succession conflicts, Berke Khan vs Ilkhanate (1260s), civil war between Nogai and Tokhta (1299–1300), and Tokhtamysh vs Timur (1390s), repeatedly mobilized the horde's resources in internecine conflict rather than external expansion.

Timur's campaigns against Tokhtamysh (1391, 1395) systematically destroyed Sarai, Azov, and the agricultural-commercial infrastructure of the western steppe. The horde never recovered economically from the destruction of its trade city network.

By 1440, the Golden Horde had fragmented into five successor khanates: Crimea, Kazan, Astrakhan, the Great Horde, and the Kazakh. These competing heirs fought each other rather than defending against Muscovite expansion.
